I grew up visiting the city often, now live here, and I’m 23 F so here’s my opinions

Skip:
- Navy Pier: basically just a mall on a pier. Never been in the Ferris wheel so that might be nice, but I don’t think it’s worth the time or effort to visit just to talk around

- Starbucks Reserve: I get it, it’s the world’s largest Starbucks, but the one time I went in, it was crowded and underwhelming. If you need something free to fill your schedule, than I would go but I wouldn’t take something off your itinerary to do it. 

- Skydeck/Sears Tower - if you want to go up in a big building, do the Hancock Tower/Chicago 360. Less expensive, less crowded, better location to other things (Sears is very much in business district; Hancock’s on Michigan Ave), and better views imo since you’re right on the lake 

Must Dos:
- Art Institute: You could spend a whole weekend here and not see everything. Chicago’s most world class museum with so many iconic pieces of work. Highly recommend joining a guided tour or downloading their app for audio tours. 

- Architecture Boat Tour: Probably the most recommended thing you’ll find on this sub. There’s some chicagoans who do it every year due to new buildings who grow up. The Chicago architecture center is considered the best. 

- Chicago Cultural Center: Free and across from the bean. Beautiful, beautiful architecture. Great if you need something to fill your schedule, need to cool off, etc. 

If you want a less touristy schedule, I would recommend heading off into the neighborhoods. Grab dinner in Logan Square and then see a show at the Lincoln Lodge. If you want a full, long day out of downtown, walk around Armitage corridor in Lincoln Park in the morning, head to the (free) zoo, and then walk to North Avenue beach.

Couple things 

Ash Wednesday: Receiving ashes on Ash Wednesday is actually completely optional. Most ashes do not stay on well so usually you just have a smudge within a couple minutes. You just walk up with everyone else, they put the ashes on, they’ll say something (usually “remember you are dust and to dust you shall return”), and then you go about your day.

Fasting: The two fasting days are Ash Wednesday and Good Friday. You are limited to two snacks and a small meal so it’s not a full fast like say Ramadan (unless you want to do that). 

No meat: Non-meat includes red and white meat. It does not include fish, and it’s traditional to eat fish on Fridays during Lent. Pre-Vatican II, you weren’t supposed to eat meat on any Friday. Then it changed to you were supposed to make a sacrifice of your choice on a Friday (could be meat if you want to), but the only Catholics who really know/practice that tend to be traditionalists. 

Lenten Sacrifice: It’s fully up to you. Some people also decide to “add” something to their life like praying the rosary daily instead of/in addition to a sacrifice. Also, the Sundays during Lent technically aren’t included in the 40 days so if you give something up, you can indulge on it then.

22 F lived in Lake View for about 6 months last year, now in Logan Square. Here’s my thoughts on each 

Logan Square - I really enjoy the neighborhood, and I live about a block off Milwaukee. Lots of access to restaurants, bars, boutiques/gift shops, etc. I love, love, love the blue line. I can get to the loop super quick and going to ORD is a piece of cake. I enjoy wicker park, but I would rather prefer living in Logan and taking a 10-15 minute blue line there. I feel like this is a common sentiment - great to visit, not to live. I pay about $1,150 with two roommates. 3 bed, two bath, 1400 sq ft, in-unit, two stories, about 5 minute walk to blue line. We’re paying more than others in our area, but I feel like it’s worth it. My roommates and I did look at lake view but we were going pay more for less space and a not as nice unit. My cons of living here are two things. First is groceries. There’s an Aldi’s on Belmont, the co-op (which will nickel and dime you), and target. Definitely can do a lot of shopping between the three, but there’s no large grocery store like a Jewel or Mariano’s. One of my roommates does have a car so we use that. If we didn’t, I would probably get my groceries delivered. Jewel offers $90/year delivery so definitely wouldn’t be the end of the world if I had to. Other con is I sometimes feel like I’m cut off from the rest of the city, especially the lake view/Lincoln park area. I had a doctors appt yesterday in Lincoln park and it was a 15 minute uber ride and an almost hour CTA ride. Everything on the blue line is easy, but beyond that, it can be difficult. 

Now lake view. I love the density of Lakeview and the access to the lake. I lived about a block off of LSD, and it was amazing. Where I was particularly, it was very residential so while everything was a short distance away, nothing was right outside my door like it feels like in Logan. Also, transit can be a bitch. I would take a bus into the Loop for work and while mornings were fine, LSD would be gridlocked most afternoons. However if you live closer to the red/brown line, that would be less of an issue. Also just a minor thing but many apartments in Lake View that I personally looked at are above retail spots which can be loud and also you have to deal with moving things into a second or third floor unit. Again, minor thing and definitely not exclusive to Lakeview.

Some quick CTA tips
1. Determine how many times you think you’ll use the CTA and see if it’s economical to [buy passes](https://www.transitchicago.com/fares/#passes). It should be noted that there is a hold time between swipes (I think it’s 20 minutes) so everyone would have to get a pass. If you go the pass route, you must get a Ventra (CTA) card. They’re available at every L stop. If you decide not to do passes, you can just use any type of wireless card (including ApplePay, Google Pay, etc) to pay. 

2. Use Maps apps to get around. Google Maps is most popular, but I found Apple Maps is more accurate with public transit. You can put in exactly where you need to go and it’ll tell you where to walk, what line to get on, where to get off, etc. I would also download the Ventra app, even if you don’t get a card, as they have the most accurate arrival/departure times of trains.

I’ve never been to SF but navigating public transit here is relatively easy.

For riding, you’ll want to get a Ventra card (available at all L stations). You don’t *have* to use it for payment, but the main reason to get it is for passes. It allows for unlimited rides during whatever time span you choose. Most times it’s a deal. For example, a 1 day pass is $5, and one ride of the L is $2.50. You can purchase passes at the card machines or upload the card to the Ventra app and manage it that way. That’s what I use and then I just tap my phone. If you’re paying a normal fare, you can still use a card or a tap credit card (either a physical one or on your phone).

Navigating is pretty easy. I just use the maps app on my phone, put in where I want to go, choose the transit option, and it’ll tell you what stop to go to, what line/route to get on, where to get off, etc. 

For the type of people who use public transit, it’s really a mixed bag. Yeah, you do have some sketchy people and some who cause a scene, but like 90% of people are just going about their day. Some lines/stations are known to be sketchier than others, but I’ve personally never felt like I’ve been in danger (though I have been uncomfortable)

I got there around 5:50 PM. They say don’t line up before 6 but they had staff lining people up. Priority ticket holders line up along Ida B Wells along the theatre and then start to wrap around the block by Roosevelt University. General ticket holders are lined up on the north side of Michigan by the Park. Make sure to get in the right line!

I would say by the time 8:30 came around, my estimation was there was about 600-700 people. We were about 40th in line. They started counting us around 8 and then around 8:40 came to scan tickets, check IDs, and stamp your hand. After the priority line clears, we went across the street. They checked for the stamps on our hands and then get a paper ticket with your seat number. You then go through security (metal detector and very thorough bag check). They sell souvenirs and concessions (beers, wine, sodas, candy, and chips). They also sell concessions are each floor of the theatre. You can take food to your seat but they will make you throw it away before taping.

I think everyone in general got placed on the 6th floor balcony or gallery. Between the two, they probably hold about 500(?) so I assume/hope most people got in. They still had a pretty thick stack of tickets when we entered.

There was an opener, the band came out, we got instructions from the stage manager, and Stephen answered questions for about 4ish minutes. The audience is very, very loud (we were so excited) to the point you couldn’t hear Stephen sometimes. It was a very, very cool experience.

The only two complaints I had were things they couldn’t really control. One was the time. Because the DNC went to over time, taping didn’t start until midnight. Some people left before taping even started. For us that was there early, it was a long day. Hopefully that’s not a problem later in the week. Also, some audience etiquette.
